posts.title: A sample post
posts.summary: An example of the new blog format, sitting where a real post will. Replace it with the first week of the season, or delete it.

sections.heading: This is a sample
sections.body:
Nothing here describes a real week. It is in place so the team can see what a post looks like on the season page and on the blog, and so there is something to copy the shape of.

Replace it with the first real post of the season, or delete it from the editor.

sections.heading: What a real one would say
sections.body:
A post is usually three or four sections. The ones that earn their place are:

- what we set out to do
- what we actually built
- what broke, and what changed because of it
- what is next

sections.heading: Where to write it
sections.body:
Open /admin, pick Build blog posts, and press Add post. A blank line starts a new paragraph and a line beginning with a dash becomes a bullet, which is the whole format.

There is a longer guide in the draft post called “How to write a build blog”.

posts.title: How to write a build blog
posts.summary: What a good build blog does, and how to write one on this site. Kept as a draft so it stays off the public list.

sections.heading: What a build blog is for
sections.body:
A build blog is the record of a season. Judges read it, other teams read it, and next year's students read it when they are trying to work out why we did something.

Write it the week it happens. A post written in April about week two is a summary; a post written in week two is evidence.

sections.heading: What goes in one
sections.body:
Aim for three or four sections. The useful ones are usually:

- what we set out to do this week
- what we actually built
- what broke, and what we changed because of it
- what we are doing next

sections.heading: Writing it here
sections.body:
Open the editor at /admin, pick Build blog posts, and press Add post. Fill in the title, the season, the date and a one-line summary, then add a section for each part of the story.

A blank line starts a new paragraph. A line starting with a dash and a space becomes a bullet, like the list above. That is the whole format.

Photos go in public/blog-images/ and are referenced with a leading slash, like /blog-images/week-1-drivetrain.jpg. Always write the description field: it is what someone using a screen reader hears, and what shows if the photo fails to load.

sections.heading: Before you publish
sections.body:
New posts start as drafts, which keeps them off the blog list and out of search engines while you work. Turn the draft switch off when it is ready.

Read it back once. Names spelled right, no half-finished sentences, and nothing that would embarrass us in front of a sponsor.
